lead: These chapters explain what an aircraft is made of and what each part is asked to do. They move from the parts and their materials to the loads those parts must survive, so that by the end you can find the critical load cases from a V-n diagram, draw the shear and bending moment along a wing, and check a fuselage and tail for pressure, bending and torsion.
about: The unit begins with the parts of an airframe and their jobs, then the two ways a shell can be built, monocoque and semi-monocoque, and how a real wing and fuselage are laid out. Honeycomb and sandwich panels follow, then the metals and composites used and how they behave. Fabrication and connections close the hardware half. The second half is about loads: limit and ultimate loads and the design rules built on them, the V-n diagram that fixes the critical load factors, shear force and bending moment along the span, and finally the stress analysis of the fuselage and tail unit, with the tail balancing load. Each chapter feeds the next: loads give the numbers, the V-n diagram gives the worst cases, and beam theory turns those cases into stresses.

chapters.idea: An aircraft is a set of load paths; every member exists to collect a load and pass it on to a stronger member.
chapters.depth: Name and locate the main groups: wing, fuselage, empennage, landing gear, engine mounts. Inside them: skin, stringers, longerons, ribs, frames, bulkheads, spars, spar caps, doublers, fittings, floor beams. For each, give the function in one line: carry load, keep aerodynamic shape, protect payload, join parts, provide access. Explain how a load travels from skin to stringer to rib to spar to fuselage. Some syllabi call the skin the 'stressed skin' or 'covering'.

figure.aria: An airframe tree showing wing, fuselage, tail and landing gear with the main members under each and the job of each member.

chapters.example: A wing skin panel 0.6 m long and 0.4 m wide has a normal pressure of 15 kPa acting on it. Four stringers share the panel load equally. Find the load carried by each stringer. Panel area = 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.24 m². Panel load = 15 000 × 0.24 = 3 600 N. Load per stringer = 3 600 / 4 = 900 N.
chapters.trap: Mixing up the roles of ribs and spars: ribs hold the shape and pass loads to the spars, spars run spanwise and take the bending.
chapters.leave: Detailed shear and bending stress in these members to Unit 4 and Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Monocoque means the skin carries everything; semi-monocoque adds a skeleton so the skin can be thin and the stringers take the bending.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities examine this as a separate topic, so keep it short. Define monocoque, semi-monocoque and the older truss (wire-braced fabric) construction. Show why a pure monocoque is heavy: a thin unstiffened shell buckles, so the skin must be thick. In semi-monocoque, the skin takes shear and pressure, stringers and longerons take bending, frames hold the shape and shorten the skin panels. Give the pressure formulas for a thin cylinder: hoop stress σ = pr/t and longitudinal stress σ = pr/2t, with p in Pa, r the radius in m and t the skin thickness in m.

figure.aria: Three construction types side by side, with the semi-monocoque branch splitting into the jobs of skin, stringers and frames.

chapters.example: A semi-monocoque fuselage has diameter 2.0 m and skin thickness 1.5 mm. The cabin differential pressure is 60 kPa. Find the hoop and longitudinal skin stresses. Radius r = 1.0 m, t = 0.0015 m. Hoop stress = pr/t = 60 000 × 1.0 / 0.0015 = 40 MPa. Longitudinal stress = pr/2t = 20 MPa.
chapters.trap: Assuming the skin of a semi-monocoque fuselage carries no load because the stringers are there; the skin still carries all the pressurisation.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1 for the names of the members.
chapters.leave: Buckling of stiffened panels to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A wing is a torsion box of spars, ribs, stringers and skin, and a fuselage is a stiffened tube with frames, longerons and pressure bulkheads.
chapters.depth: Draw a typical two-spar wing: front and rear spar, spar caps, ribs at a pitch, stringers on the upper and lower skin, skin panels, trailing edge and leading edge. Show the torsion box between the spars. Cover the fuselage: frames at a pitch, longerons, skin, floor beams, pressure bulkheads at the ends of the cabin, cut-outs for doors and wheel wells. Explain that cut-outs need doublers and that shape must be kept for aerodynamic reasons. Keep section stress calculations out of this chapter.

figure.title: Wing box load path
figure.aria: A chain from top skin through stringers, ribs and spar to the root joint, showing how a wing panel load reaches the fuselage.

chapters.example: A wing has chord 3.0 m over a semi-span part of 4.5 m. The front spar is at 15% chord and the rear spar at 60% chord, and ribs sit at 0.45 m pitch. Find the width of the torsion box and the number of ribs. Box width = (0.60 − 0.15) × 3.0 = 1.35 m. Number of bays = 4.5 / 0.45 = 10, so there are 11 ribs counting the root rib.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that a cut-out such as a door or wheel well removes skin and must be reinforced, and counting bays as ribs.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1 and the shell ideas of Chapter 2.
chapters.leave: Sandwich panels to Chapter 4; shear flow in the box to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Two thin stiff faces glued to a light core give very high bending stiffness for very little weight.
chapters.depth: Describe the sandwich: two face sheets, a core of hexagonal honeycomb, foam or balsa, and the adhesive layers that join them. Explain that faces act like the flanges of an I-beam (tension and compression) and the core acts like the web (shear) and holds the faces apart. Give the per-unit-width bending stiffness D = E_f t_f d²/2, where E_f is the face modulus in Pa, t_f the face thickness in m and d the distance between face mid-planes in m, about core thickness plus face thickness. List failure modes: face yielding, face wrinkling, core shear, core crushing, debonding. Mention uses: floor panels, control surfaces, radomes, helicopter blades.

figure.aria: A layer stack of face sheet, adhesive, honeycomb core, adhesive and face sheet, top to bottom.

chapters.example: A sandwich panel has two aluminium faces 0.5 mm thick (E = 70 GPa) on a 20 mm core. Find D per metre width and compare with a solid aluminium sheet of the same mass per unit area. Core plus one face: d = 20 + 0.5 = 20.5 mm = 0.0205 m. D = E t d²/2 = 70 × 10⁹ × 0.0005 × 0.0205² / 2 = 7.35 kN·m per metre width. Same mass gives a 1.0 mm solid sheet: D = E t³/12 = 70 × 10⁹ × (0.001)³ / 12 = 5.8 N·m. The sandwich is about 1 260 times stiffer.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the core entirely and quoting only the faces' own bending stiffness, or ignoring core shear and debonding as failure modes.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3 for skin-stringer panels; simple bending from Unit 4.
chapters.leave: Composite laminates and orthotropic plies to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Material choice is a trade of strength, stiffness, weight, fatigue life, temperature limit, corrosion and cost.
chapters.depth: Cover aluminium alloys 2024, 7075 and 6061 with their uses, magnesium, titanium Ti-6Al-4V, high-strength steels for landing gear, and composites CFRP and GFRP. Give density, modulus, yield and ultimate strength ranges in standard values. Define specific strength σ/ρ and specific stiffness E/ρ, with σ in Pa and ρ in kg/m³. Discuss fatigue, stress corrosion, galvanic corrosion between carbon fibre and aluminium, temperature limits of aluminium and composites, and repairability. Do not teach laminate theory here.

figure.aria: A family tree of aerospace materials with the common alloys and composites under each family and a short note on where each is used.

chapters.example: Compare the specific strength σ_ult/ρ of three materials: 7075-T6 aluminium with σ_ult = 570 MPa and ρ = 2 810 kg/m³; Ti-6Al-4V with 950 MPa and 4 430 kg/m³; CFRP with 1 500 MPa and 1 600 kg/m³. Aluminium: 570 × 10⁶ / 2 810 = 203 kN·m/kg. Titanium: 950 × 10⁶ / 4 430 = 214 kN·m/kg. CFRP: 1 500 × 10⁶ / 1 600 = 938 kN·m/kg. Carbon fibre wins on this ratio but loses on compressive strength, temperature and repair.
chapters.trap: Quoting yield strength where ultimate is meant, and comparing on strength alone without density, fatigue and temperature.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4 for why light stiff faces matter.
chapters.leave: Layup, ply orientation and laminate stiffness to Unit 6; fatigue detail to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Parts are formed, machined or laid up, then joined, and the joint, not the plate, usually decides the strength.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities examine fabrication as a full topic, so keep it brief and exam-oriented. Routes: sheet forming and stretch forming, machining a spar from a solid billet, extrusion, composite layup and autoclave cure. Joining: rivets, bolts, adhesive bonding, seam welding, and the fittings that transfer load between parts. Treat connections as a joint problem: lap and butt joints, load transfer through a group of fasteners, bearing and net-section checks, eccentricity in a single lap, hole fatigue, interference fit and sealant. One worked rivet-group sum is enough.

figure.title: Fabrication route
figure.aria: A top-to-bottom route from raw stock through forming or machining, surface treatment, jig assembly, joining and inspection.

chapters.example: A single lap joint uses 4 rivets of 4 mm diameter. The allowable shear stress per rivet is 200 MPa. Find the load the joint can carry if all rivets share equally. Rivet area = π × 0.004² / 4 = 1.257 × 10⁻⁵ m². Load per rivet = 200 × 10⁶ × 1.257 × 10⁻⁵ = 2 513 N. Total for 4 rivets = 10 052 N, about 10 kN, and the real joint carries less because of eccentricity and bearing on the sheet.
chapters.trap: Treating a riveted or bonded joint as if the sheet were continuous; the net section with holes and the bearing stress often govern, not rivet shear.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5 for the material allowables; Chapter 1 for which members are joined.
chapters.leave: Fatigue of joints to Unit 3; composite layup theory to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Flight and ground loads are converted to design loads by a load factor and a factor of safety, and the structure is sized for the worst combination.
chapters.depth: Cover the sources of load: lift, weight and inertia, thrust and drag, gust, landing impact, ground handling, cabin pressure, and control surface loads. Define limit load (the largest expected in service) and ultimate load (1.5 × limit for aircraft, the factor of safety), with the load factor n = L/W dimensionless. Explain inertia relief: the mass of the aircraft balances the aerodynamic load, so the net load on a section is the difference, not the aerodynamic load alone. Introduce design criteria: safe-life, fail-safe, damage tolerance, and the idea of a critical load case.

figure.title: From load to design
figure.aria: A chain from flight and ground loads to limit load, the 1.5 factor, ultimate load and the member design.

chapters.example: An aircraft of mass 60 000 kg is designed for a manoeuvre load factor of 2.5. Find the limit lift and the ultimate load for a wing. Weight W = 60 000 × 9.81 = 588.6 kN. Limit lift = nW = 2.5 × 588.6 = 1.47 MN. Ultimate load = 1.5 × 1.47 = 2.21 MN.
chapters.trap: Applying the 1.5 factor of safety to already-factored numbers, or forgetting that inertia relief reduces the net load on an internal section.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 1 and 3 for which member sees which load.
chapters.leave: Failure theories and fatigue life to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: The V-n diagram plots the load factor the aircraft can reach at each speed, and its corners give the cases that size the wing.
chapters.depth: Build the diagram step by step: the stall line n = (V/V_S1)² where V_S1 is the one-g stall speed, the positive limit n_max and negative limit, the manoeuvre speed V_A where the stall line meets n_max, cruise speed V_C and dive speed V_D, and the gust lines n = 1 ± ρ V a U /(2 W/S) with ρ in kg/m³, V in m/s, a the lift curve slope per radian, U the gust velocity in m/s and W/S the wing loading in N/m². Superimpose gust and manoeuvre envelopes and read off the critical corner. Explain how the critical n and the speed at which it occurs size the wing, fuselage and tail.

figure.aria: A V-n diagram with the stall line rising as speed squared, a flat top at load factor 2.5 from the manoeuvre speed to cruise speed, and a gust line crossing it.

chapters.example: A wing has loading W/S = 3 000 N/m² and C_Lmax = 1.5 in air of density 1.225 kg/m³. The design load factor is 2.5. Find the one-g stall speed and the manoeuvre speed V_A. V_S1 = √(2(W/S) / (ρ C_Lmax)) = √(6 000 / (1.225 × 1.5)) = √3 265 = 57.1 m/s. V_A = V_S1 √n_max = 57.1 × √2.5 = 90.3 m/s. Above 90.3 m/s the wing stalls before it reaches n = 2.5, so the corner (90.3 m/s, 2.5) sizes the wing bending.
chapters.trap: Drawing the stall line as a straight line, or forgetting the negative-g half of the diagram and the gust lines that can sit above the manoeuvre envelope at high speed.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7 for limit load and load factor.
chapters.leave: The bending moment that this load factor produces along the wing to Chapter 9.

chapters.idea: Treat the wing as a cantilever and integrate the net spanwise load to get the shear force and bending moment diagrams.
chapters.depth: Take the spanwise lift distribution, subtract the wing structural mass and fuel distribution to get the net load per unit span w(x) in N/m. Then V(x) = ∫w dx and M(x) = ∫V dx, with the tip free so V and M vanish at the tip and are largest at the root. Show Schrenk's approximation for the lift distribution as the mean of the elliptic and the planform distributions. Cover taper, effect of fuel in the wing, the fuselage carry-through, and the fuselage bending moment produced by tail loads. Keep the cross-section stress work out of this chapter.

figure.aria: Shear force and bending moment along a wing semi-span, both falling to zero at the tip and largest at the root, with moment the larger quantity.

chapters.example: A wing of semi-span 8 m carries a uniform lift of 12 kN/m and has wing structure and fuel of 3 kN/m along the same span. Find the shear force and bending moment at the root and at 2 m from the root. Net load = 12 − 3 = 9 kN/m. At the root: shear = 9 × 8 = 72 kN, moment = 9 × 8²/2 = 288 kN·m. At x = 2 m from the root the length left is 6 m: shear = 9 × 6 = 54 kN, moment = 9 × 6²/2 = 162 kN·m.
chapters.trap: Leaving out mass relief, which reduces the root moment, and mixing the sign convention so the moment diagram comes out upside down.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7 and Chapter 8 for the load factor that scales the lift.
chapters.leave: Stress distribution over the cross-section, stringers and skew loads to Unit 4; shear flow and torsion to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: The fuselage is a beam under bending, shear and pressure, and the tail unit feeds bending and torsion into the rear fuselage.
chapters.depth: Idealise the fuselage as a thin tube with longerons carrying bending and skin carrying shear and pressure. Give hoop stress pr/t and longitudinal stress pr/2t, then add the bending stress from M r/I with I ≈ π r³ t for a thin tube. Show that hoop and longitudinal stresses act at right angles, so combine them with a von Mises or principal stress check rather than adding them. Cover frames under concentrated loads, cut-out reinforcement, pressure bulkhead loads. For the tail: the tailplane balancing load bends the rear fuselage, the fin side load bends and twists the fin and its root joint. Keep torsion theory to Unit 5.

figure.title: Fuselage and tail load paths
figure.aria: Two branches, one from the tailplane load through the fin root into rear fuselage bending, and one from cabin pressure to skin hoop stress, meeting at a combined stress check.

chapters.example: A fuselage has radius 1.2 m and skin 1.6 mm thick. The cabin differential pressure is 55 kPa and the ultimate bending moment at the section is 200 kN·m. Find the longitudinal stress. Hoop stress = pr/t = 55 000 × 1.2 / 0.0016 = 41.3 MPa. Longitudinal pressure stress = pr/2t = 20.6 MPa. Second moment of area of the thin tube I = π r³ t = π × 1.2³ × 0.0016 = 8.69 × 10⁻³ m⁴. Bending stress = M r / I = 200 000 × 1.2 / 8.69 × 10⁻³ = 27.6 MPa. Total longitudinal stress = 20.6 + 27.6 = 48.2 MPa, below the 2024 aluminium yield of about 345 MPa.
chapters.trap: Adding the hoop stress straight into the longitudinal total; the two act at right angles and must be combined through a biaxial failure check.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 9 for bending moments and shear; Chapter 2 for the pressure formulas.
chapters.leave: Shear flow, shear centre and Bredt-Batho torsion to Unit 5; buckling of the skin to Unit 6.
